guide.title: Gastrointestinal & Abdominal Emergencies
guide.lead: You won't make the final diagnosis, but you can find the dangerous belly: shock, a rigid abdomen, a pulsatile mass, blood, or pain far worse than the examination. Keep them nil by mouth, treat pain and nausea, and transport the right way.

sections.title: Where it hurts
rows: Central, moving to the right lower quadrant
Right upper quadrant to the shoulder, after fatty food
Epigastric through to the back, better leaning forward
Colicky, distended, vomiting, no stool or gas
Sudden abdominal or back pain with collapse
Lower abdominal pain and fainting, childbearing age
Severe pain, soft belly (pain out of proportion)

groups.title: Peritonitis
items: Lies still; guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness

groups.title: Bleeding
items: Vomited blood or coffee grounds; black tarry stool (upper)
Dizzy or BP drops on sitting up: significant loss

groups.title: Hidden disease
items: Older adults, diabetes, steroids: little pain, serious disease

steps.title: Recognise
steps.text: Men over 65, smokers, hypertension; sudden pain, collapse, pulsatile mass.

steps.title: Permissive hypotension
steps.text: If conscious, accept systolic about 70–90 mmHg.

steps.title: Go
steps.text: Straight to a vascular surgery centre with pre-notification.

sections.title: Every abdominal patient
items: Shock: treat as hemorrhage (see Shock & Hemorrhage)

quiz.q: Pain started around the navel 8 hours ago and moved to the right lower quadrant; nausea, low fever. Most likely?
quiz.explanation: Migration to the right lower quadrant is classic.

quiz.q: Hypertensive smoker, 70, with sudden tearing abdominal pain to the back, pale, BP 90/58, pulsatile mass. Action?
options: Don't palpate deeply; gentle, rapid transport to a vascular surgery centre

quiz.q: On warfarin: coffee-ground vomit, black stools, BP 104/68 lying and 84/52 sitting. Means:
options: Significant upper GI bleed with major blood loss
quiz.explanation: Lie flat, IV access en route, close monitoring.
They lie still because movement hurts.
Bright red or maroon blood suggests a lower source.

quiz.q: Epigastric pain to the back, eased by leaning forward, after heavy drinking:
quiz.explanation: Gallstones are the other common cause.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old woman has lower abdominal pain and fainted. Must consider:
Permissive hypotension target in a conscious patient with ruptured aortic aneurysm:
Severe abdominal pain with a soft, barely tender abdomen in an older patient with AF:
quiz.explanation: Pain out of proportion is the clue.

flashcards.question: Melena vs hematochezia
flashcards.answer: Melena: black tarry stool, upper GI bleed. Hematochezia: bright red or maroon blood, usually lower GI bleed.

flashcards.question: Appendicitis
flashcards.answer: Central pain moving to the right lower quadrant, nausea, loss of appetite, low-grade fever.

flashcards.question: Cholecystitis
flashcards.answer: Right upper quadrant pain to the right shoulder, often after fatty food, with nausea and fever.

flashcards.question: Pancreatitis
flashcards.answer: Epigastric pain through to the back, better leaning forward, vomiting. Gallstones and alcohol.

flashcards.question: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
flashcards.answer: Sudden abdominal, back or flank pain, collapse, pulsatile mass. Don't palpate deeply; gentle handling; vascular surgery centre.

flashcards.question: GI bleed with shock
flashcards.answer: Lie flat, oxygen to target, IV access en route, nothing by mouth, rapid transport. Bring the medication list (anticoagulants, NSAIDs).

flashcards.question: Pain out of proportion to examination
flashcards.answer: Think mesenteric ischemia, especially in older patients with AF or vascular disease.

critical.scenario: A 24-year-old lies very still. Pain started centrally 4 hours ago and is now right lower. Vomited twice. HR 102, temperature 38.1 °C. The right lower quadrant is rigid and he flinches when you release pressure.
critical.question: What does this suggest, and management?

options.t: Appendicitis with peritonitis: nothing by mouth, position of comfort, analgesia and antiemetic per protocol, transport
Let him walk to the ambulance

critical.explanation: Fever and rising heart rate suggest the inflammation is progressing.
critical.kpi: Recognizes peritoneal signs including guarding, rigidity, and rebound tenderness

critical.scenario: An 82-year-old taking naproxen has black stools; sitting up drops BP from 100/64 to 84/50 and he vomits coffee-ground material.
critical.question: Source and management?

options.t: Upper GI bleed (likely NSAID ulcer) with major blood loss: lie flat, oxygen to target, IV access en route, rapid transport

options.f: Coffee grounds and melena are upper GI.

options.t: Sit him up to stop vomiting

critical.explanation: Older patients decompensate fast; bring the naproxen.
critical.kpi: Recognizes upper GI bleeding from melena and hematemesis with orthostatic hypotension

critical.scenario: A 72-year-old heavy smoker collapsed with sudden ripping lower abdominal and back pain. BP 82/56, HR 118, confused. A firm pulsatile mass above the navel.
critical.question: Diagnosis and priority?

options.t: Ruptured aortic aneurysm: no deep palpation, minimal handling, accept systolic about 70–90 mmHg, rapid transport to vascular surgery
Kidney stone: analgesia and routine transport
options.f: Shock and a pulsatile mass mean rupture.

options.t: Large fluid boluses to normal BP

critical.explanation: Don't delay transport for IV access.
critical.kpi: Identifies ruptured AAA by the triad of shock, tearing pain, and pulsatile mass
